articles.headline: U.S. Posts Near-$2 Trillion Deficit, Its 25th Straight Year of Spending More Than It Has
articles.dek: The Treasury's $1.992 trillion shortfall is up 12% from last year, and interest on the debt alone now tops $1 trillion.
articles.catch_up: The federal government's fiscal year ended September 30, and Treasury has released the final tally. Long-term bond yields have climbed above 5% this year, as the war with Iran, heavy borrowing and AI-related corporate debt compete for investors' money.
articles.why_it_matters: Higher Treasury yields feed directly into mortgage rates, which are around 7.5%, and into the government's own borrowing costs. With divided government expected after the midterms, a fix looks years away.
body: The United States ended fiscal 2026 with a budget deficit of $1.992 trillion, the Treasury Department reported Friday. That is about 12% above last year's $1.775 trillion, and the third-largest in American history, behind only the two pandemic stimulus years of 2020 and 2021. According to CNBC, this is the 25th consecutive year in the red. The last surplus came in 2001, a year many staffers now in government were still learning to read.

Translation: a deficit is the gap between what the government collects and what it spends in a year. Treasury also reported record receipts and record outlays, which is a way of saying the government has never taken in so much money and has still managed to fall this far short of it.

The biggest line items are familiar. Social Security cost nearly $1.7 trillion, Medicare almost $1.1 trillion, and net interest, meaning what Treasury pays on its debt minus what it receives, topped $1 trillion for the first time in the sources' accounting, up from $970 billion. Gross interest on the national debt exceeded $1.3 trillion. The national debt passed $40 trillion earlier this year and has more than doubled in a decade. The government is now spending more on the cost of having borrowed money than on most things it actually bought with it.

On the revenue side, individual income taxes brought in more than $2.8 trillion, up about 7%. Corporate income tax fell by roughly $70 billion to $381 billion, which CNBC attributes to the tax cuts in last year's One Big Beautiful Bill act. Tariffs set a record for gross customs duties, but net customs revenue took a hit because the Supreme Court ruled many of the tariffs unconstitutional, forcing refunds of billions of dollars to retailers. The White House has kept raising levies anyway. A revenue plan that must be partly paid back is a novel concept.

The administration's stated answer is growth. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in Dallas last month: "we have to grow our way out of it." CNBC's analysis cites the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, which calculates that balancing the budget on growth alone would take a decade of 7.2% annual growth. Second-quarter GDP was recently revised up to 2.2% at an annualized rate. The distance between 2.2% and 7.2% is what economists call a gap and what everyone else calls a hope.

Bessent has also argued for a deficit below 4% of GDP by the end of Trump's term. The current deficit is about 6.2% of GDP, per CNBC's estimate. The analysis calls hitting the target almost impossible.

Markets are already charging for the habit. The 10-year Treasury yield stood at 5.1% as of October 15, up 114 basis points since the end of February. Translation: a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so the cost of lending to Washington for a decade has risen by about 1.14 points. CNBC ties the rise to the war with Iran that began Feb. 28, higher oil and diesel prices, heavy Treasury issuance, and companies borrowing hundreds of billions to build AI infrastructure. Brent crude was at $126.55 in the latest data. Mortgage rates track the 10-year, and Redfin reported pending home sales fell 4% in September, the biggest monthly drop in three years.

The Congressional Budget Office estimates that if rates run a half-point above its forecast, deficits over ten years grow by $1.9 trillion. A 1.5-point overshoot adds $6 trillion. The CBO expects the 10-year to average 4.3%, against 5.1% today.

The political outlook is not helping. Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House in the Nov. 3 midterms. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next Democratic speaker, wants to reverse $1 trillion in healthcare cuts enacted last year. Trump, meanwhile, pledged $5,000 checks to every adult citizen if Republicans swept the election. CNBC notes the parties are far apart and mutually hostile.

The analysis does offer some comfort: higher yields also attract buyers to Treasuries, and expensive borrowing is not the same as a crisis. Its conclusion is that economics alone cannot solve this, and the politics need fixing too. Both are currently scheduled for after the election, then after the next one.
articles.wire_headline: U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year

articles.headline: Chip Index Posts Longest Losing Streak Since 2008 as AI Trade Meets Its Invoice
articles.dek: The Nasdaq had its worst week since June, the VIX topped 22, and traders bought bets that fear will last through November.
articles.catch_up: Stocks tied to artificial intelligence sold off last week as inflation ran hotter than expected and worries grew about how much debt companies are taking on to build AI infrastructure. Chip stocks, neocloud providers like CoreWeave and cybersecurity names were hit hardest.
articles.why_it_matters: If inflation keeps borrowing costs high, the debt-funded AI buildout gets more expensive, and the index funds in many retirement accounts hold a lot of AI-linked stocks. Diversification, long considered boring, briefly looked clever.
body: The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, known as SOX, posted its longest losing streak since 2008, according to Investing.com. CNBC reported that the iShares Semiconductor ETF fell nine straight sessions, its longest run in more than a decade. Translation: an ETF is a basket of stocks you can buy in one click, and this basket went down nine days in a row.

The Nasdaq fell 4.5% for the week, ending a four-week winning streak and marking its worst week since June, CNBC said. The S&P 500 fell 2%, while the Dow rose 0.7% as investors moved into healthcare, consumer staples and other sectors that do not depend on a chatbot. The Dow, a collection of old companies that sell things people physically need, had a rare moment of being the sensible one.

The sell-off sped up Wednesday after September consumer prices rose 3.7% from a year earlier, against the 3.6% economists expected. Translation: prices are rising faster than hoped, so the Federal Reserve may keep interest rates high for longer. The next day, producer prices, what businesses pay for inputs, jumped 1.3% on the month and 6.3% on the year. CNBC noted those were the largest annual and monthly gains since March 2022 and December 2022, respectively, and said elevated oil prices were part of the cause.

That matters because the AI buildout runs on borrowed money. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan warned Monday that access to capital could become the industry's next major constraint, CNBC reported. In an industry that has spent years saying the only limit was chips, discovering that the limit is also money is a modest plot twist.

CoreWeave, a so-called neocloud that rents out computing power, was the week's cautionary tale. CNBC said its total debt has risen to more than $51 billion and its stock fell 25% for the week, including a 13% drop on Friday. More worrying than the stock, the network said, were rising yields on its corporate bonds and a spike in credit default swaps. Translation: a credit default swap is insurance against a borrower not paying you back, and the price of that insurance went up.

Memory chipmakers Micron, Sandisk, Western Digital and Seagate also fell after China's CXMT announced progress on a more efficient chip structure, which raised fears of more competition and a glut of supply. Cybersecurity stocks suffered too. Palo Alto Networks lost more than 18% and CrowdStrike more than 17%, partly on reports that OpenAI is in early talks to buy Trail of Bits, CNBC said.

The Cboe Volatility Index, or VIX, often called Wall Street's fear gauge, rose above 22 for the first time in four months. CNBC reported that one trader bought 9,200 November 20-strike calls for $1.7 million and 12,500 23-strike calls for $1.1 million. Translation: these are bets that the VIX will still be elevated in mid-November, which is a way of paying money to be nervous on schedule. Of the ten most popular VIX contracts Friday, nine were calls.

Not everyone had a bad week. Meta rallied on new AI models before ending the week down slightly, and Microsoft hit a record high Tuesday for the first time in nearly a year after a drop of more than a third. Goldman Sachs reported equities trading revenue up 72%, though bank shares still struggled, which CNBC's Jim Cramer attributed to worry about what lies ahead rather than what banks just earned.

The latest official data shows the VIX at 16.46 on October 15, well below the intraday highs CNBC described, so the fear gauge has already cooled. The 10-year Treasury yield was 5.1% and Brent crude was 126.55, which is a lot of reasons for the Fed to stay put. Next week Tesla, SpaceX and Meta report earnings, and the market will find out whether it can still be impressed by large numbers.
articles.wire_headline: Chip index SOX posts longest losing streak since 2008 as AI worries deepen

articles.headline: Markets Bet Fed Will Hold in October, Unaware Chairman Has Declined to Say
articles.dek: Futures price just a 15% chance of a hike on Oct. 28, but Kevin Warsh has rejected the habit of telling investors his plans in advance, CNBC reported.
articles.catch_up: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates unanimously in September under new chairman Kevin Warsh, who has argued inflation is a bigger worry than the job market. The committee next meets on Oct. 28.
articles.why_it_matters: If the Fed hikes when markets expect a pause, borrowing costs and asset prices could move sharply and quickly. Mortgage, loan and savings rates all follow the Fed, so a surprise reaches households as well as traders.
body: Traders are betting heavily that the Federal Reserve will leave interest rates alone when it meets later this month. According to CNBC analysis, futures markets gave a 15% probability to an October hike as of Friday morning. That leaves an 85% chance of nothing happening, which is the kind of confidence markets usually reserve for things the Fed has explicitly promised.

The Fed has not promised it. Chairman Kevin Warsh said at an International Monetary Fund event in Bangkok that he was not signaling a decision either way. Translation: the person who decides has declined to say what he will decide, and the market has filled in the blank with a guess it feels good about.

The guess rests on habit. Fed Vice Chairman Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams recently said they saw little urgency to raise rates, and markets quickly repriced toward a hold. Warsh, Jefferson and Williams form an informal leadership group known as the troika. Historically, when the troika's other two members speak, they speak for the chair. CNBC notes that outsiders cannot be sure that convention survived the change in leadership.

Warsh has also been tidy about distancing himself from the committee's paperwork. The Fed's September Summary of Economic Projections showed the median official expecting one more hike in 2026, which left room to pause in October and move in December. Asked about it at his September press conference, Warsh said, "Those aren't my forecasts." Translation: the document investors use to guess the Fed's path is, by the chairman's own account, not necessarily his path.

Then there is the inflation data. Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year through September, and producer prices rose 6.3%. CNBC says that implies core personal consumption expenditures, the Fed's preferred gauge, will come in around 3.1%. The Fed's goal is 2%, which Warsh called in Jackson Hole "a firm, fixed target." A firm, fixed target is hard to describe as met when you are at 3.1%.

Warsh also said in Bangkok that the world has "broadly conformed to our expectations" since September, which could mean the hot readings do not worry him. It could also mean something else. CNBC's analysis is that we can infer his thinking, but will not really know until the press conference after the meeting.

Current conditions do not make the choice easier. The federal funds rate sits at 3.88%, the 10-year Treasury yields 5.1%, and Brent crude is at 126.55. Unemployment is 4.2%. Markets, meanwhile, are calm: the VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, stood at 16.46. Translation: investors are relaxed, which is the condition in which surprises do the most damage.

CNBC points out that a hike against strong market expectations is a recipe for volatility, and could dent the credibility of Jefferson and Williams if they were seen to have guided investors wrongly. Warsh could instead drift toward the committee's middle once he gauges its views. Watch Oct. 28, when the chairman will at last communicate something, in the traditional manner, after the decision.
articles.wire_headline: Analysis: Everyone expects the Fed to hold rates in October. Kevin Warsh could surprise us all

articles.headline: Tesla Shows Hovering Roadster, Traders Bet Elon Will Merge His Companies
articles.dek: A car nine years late and a rocket company worth $2 trillion have pushed prediction-market odds of a Tesla-SpaceX merger above 50% for early 2027.
articles.catch_up: Tesla unveiled its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday at a SpaceX test site in Texas, almost a decade after it began taking deposits. Both companies are controlled by Elon Musk, and merger speculation has swirled since SpaceX went public in June.
articles.why_it_matters: A Tesla-SpaceX combination would merge two of the 12 U.S. companies worth at least $1 trillion, affecting index funds and shareholders who own either one. The car itself is unlikely to matter financially, but the corporate plumbing behind it could.
body: Tesla showed off its next-generation Roadster on Thursday, a little under a decade after it started collecting $50,000 deposits for the car. According to CNBC, the white prototype raced up a curved ramp, clung to it upside down, vaulted off, flipped in mid-air and hovered before landing. Tesla's own timer put zero to 60 mph at under a second. Production, Musk said, begins in 2028, which in Roadster time is practically tomorrow.

The hovering relies on SpaceX technology, including thrusters, pressure vessels and powerful fans. Translation: the car is partly a rocket, which raises the question of what exactly the customers' deposits bought. Musk conceded that "This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car," and CNBC reported it was unclear whether the vehicle would be street-legal. No price was announced.

The delivery record is its own genre. Tesla has missed every targeted date since 2017, including a demo Musk hoped to hold before the end of 2025. Sam Altman, who got his refund, wrote last year that "7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait." Others stayed in line. One reservation holder told CNBC that his $250,000 Founder's Edition deposit amounted to an "interest-free loan" to Tesla, and after the show called what he saw "off the charts." Translation: the loan is still outstanding, but the demo was good.

The Roadster is not the main event. CNBC noted it is unlikely to have a material financial impact, as a high-end, low-volume car. The real audience was the market, which has been guessing whether Tesla and SpaceX will merge. Tesla is valued at about $1.4 trillion and SpaceX at about $2 trillion. The companies already pay each other, share some personnel, and answer to the same man, so a merger would mostly be a formality in the sense that a wedding is a formality for a couple who already share a mortgage.

On Wednesday, Barclays analyst Dan Levy wrote that a deal could come before the end of 2026, and before Tesla's annual meeting, due by Dec. 6. He suggested it might be pitched as AI vertical integration, tying Tesla's Robotaxi and Optimus to SpaceX's Grok and Macrohard, with the Terafab chip project as a possible driver. Translation: vertical integration means owning every step of the process, which is easier when you already own most of the steps. Levy said the true value would be there rather than in financial synergies. SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell told CNBC before the IPO that a merger "might make Elon's life a little easier."

Traders took the hint. On a Kalshi contract asking when the two will merge, odds of a deal before March jumped to 56% by Friday morning from 29%, according to CNBC. CNBC disclosed that it has a commercial relationship with Kalshi, including a minority investment. Also Friday, Evercore ISI recommended buying SpaceX ahead of its early-November earnings and raised its price target by 20% to $275.

Next up is Tesla's third-quarter report, due after the bell on Wednesday. Investors may learn more about the overlap Musk has described on earnings calls. They may also learn whether the Roadster date, like its predecessors, has room to move.
articles.wire_headline: Tesla unveils long-delayed Roadster developed with SpaceX, fueling merger speculation

articles.headline: Berkshire Buys Into Bending Spoons, Proving Even Patience Has a Price-to-Earnings Ratio
articles.dek: Berkshire Hathaway has put about $930 million into an Italian software consolidator that buys fallen tech names, and its shares are near record highs.
articles.catch_up: Warren Buffett said in May 2025 that he would step down as CEO at year-end, and Berkshire shares then fell more than 14% over three months. Greg Abel now runs the company and its roughly $360 billion cash pile, and he has started spending some of it.
articles.why_it_matters: The deal suggests Berkshire is willing to leave its comfort zone for tech, while the software industry's decline is feeding a new kind of buyer whose model often means layoffs and price increases for customers. Investors in Berkshire, and users of Evernote or Airtable, are all affected.
body: Berkshire Hathaway shares closed Friday at their highest level since Warren Buffett announced his plan to step down, according to CNBC. The Class A shares ended at $798,000, 1.4% below their all-time closing high of $809,350. The Class B shares finished at $532.02. It is a recovery of sorts: the stock lost more than 14% after Buffett's announcement, as investors feared a 'Buffett premium' was evaporating. Translation: people had been paying extra for Buffett himself, and then wondered what they were left holding.

The stock's rise has several explanations, and only one of them involves a decision. CNBC cited analyst Meyer Shields of Keefe, Bruyette & Woods, who said higher short-term interest rates help, because Berkshire's roughly $360 billion in cash earns more. The Fed funds rate sits at 3.88%, and the 2-year Treasury yields 4.77%, so sitting still pays well. A quiet hurricane season has helped its insurance operations. Chevron, a $19 billion holding, hit a record after gaining almost 36% since July, with Brent crude at $126.55. Coca-Cola, now a $37.6 billion holding, also closed at a record.

The decision is Bending Spoons. On Wednesday the Milan-based company disclosed that Berkshire is investing a 'further' $330 million by buying 10 million new shares at $33, a discount of almost 12% to Tuesday's close of $37.86. The word 'further' was news in itself. The release also disclosed, apparently for the first time, that Berkshire put $600 million into the company's July IPO. Translation: Berkshire had been quietly a shareholder for three months, and nobody noticed until it bought more.

Bending Spoons stock rose 41% on Wednesday to $53.46. It closed Friday at $47.07, which CNBC calculates is 42.6% above Berkshire's $33 price. The CNBC newsletter author's estimate is that Berkshire holds about 30.7 million shares, worth more than $1.4 billion, a gain of 55.3% on $930 million. That assumes the $29 IPO price, and the company would not confirm the math. The September 30 portfolio disclosure next month should settle it.

What does Bending Spoons do? Founded in 2013, it buys older internet companies, including AOL, Evernote, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Brightcove, uses AI to cut costs, and spends the savings on more acquisitions. CNBC reported it recently agreed to buy Airtable for about $1.3 billion, almost 90% below its late-2021 peak valuation, and Miro for $1.36 billion, against a former valuation of $17.5 billion. Bending Spoons said a 'large portion' of Airtable's pre-acquisition team would leave with 'substantial separation packages.' Translation: the company buys the software and often not all of the people who wrote it.

The setting is what some call the 'SaaSpocalypse': AI tools displace software-as-a-service products, and the shares of Intuit, HubSpot and Adobe are each down at least 30% this year. Private equity firms such as Thoma Bravo and Vista, former big buyers, are constrained, according to former Gainsight CEO Nick Mehta, because they 'got their nose bloodied.' Bending Spoons says it hasn't lost a bidding contest in several years. Mehta said 'Bending Spooned' has become a verb in Silicon Valley, meaning to be bought for pennies on the dollar.

Customers are part of the model. After acquiring Evernote, Bending Spoons raised the annual personal subscription price to $130 from $70 in April 2023. Mizuho analyst Lloyd Walmsley said he considered switching to OneNote but stayed, because switching costs outweighed the price. That is the business thesis in miniature: own something people find annoying to leave.

Analysts are divided on the surprise. Morningstar's Greggory Warren called it, along with a $36 billion Alphabet stake, a sign Berkshire is 'finally moving out of its comfort zone.' Barron's Andrew Bary noted that many holders wanted more stock buying but that Bending Spoons was a surprise given its high valuation. Revenue more than doubled to over $700 million in the first public quarter, with growth almost entirely from acquisitions. Whether the model works when the acquisitions stop is the question the market will answer, and Berkshire's $930 million will wait for the result with its usual patience.
articles.wire_headline: Berkshire shares buck market sell-off, rally to highest since Buffett said he would step down as CEO
